questions.question: What is the central shared-responsibility invariant for an Azure workload?
options: Microsoft owns every application authorization and recovery decision
The customer owns only its monthly invoice
Azure operates the platform boundary while the workload team still owns architecture, access, data, recovery, and cost controls
A managed service eliminates the need for application observability
questions.explanation: Managed services move infrastructure tasks to Microsoft, but workload correctness, authorization, recovery objectives, configuration, and user outcomes remain customer responsibilities.

questions.question: Where should an Azure Policy assignment live?
options: Always on the tenant root regardless of impact
At the highest scope where the rule is true for every descendant, with explicit reviewed exceptions
Only on individual resources after deployment
Inside application source code instead of Resource Manager
questions.explanation: Policy inherits downward. Placing it at the highest consistently valid scope gives broad protection without forcing unrelated descendants into an incorrect rule.

questions.question: A service needs 4,200 peak requests/s. One instance sustains 420 requests/s, and target utilization is 65%. What is the minimum instance count before redundancy floors?
questions.explanation: Divide 4,200 by 420 x 0.65, which is about 15.38, then round up to 16 instances. Failure-domain and rollout headroom may require more.

questions.question: Why is a paired Azure region not a complete disaster-recovery plan?
options: Paired regions cannot run Azure services
Pairing does not automatically replicate, route, authorize, size, or validate the complete workload
Availability zones already protect against every regional failure
Only virtual machines can use paired regions
questions.explanation: Each service has its own multiregion behavior. The team must design data replication, routing, identity, quota, dependencies, failover authority, and recovery testing.

questions.question: Which control best protects against a privileged operator deletion that live replication copies to another region?
options: Add more read replicas
Increase compute autoscaling
Keep an isolated, retained backup and test restoration to a prior correct state
Route through Azure Front Door
questions.explanation: Replication preserves availability but faithfully copies valid deletes and corruption. Historical, isolated recovery provides a previous correct point.

questions.question: Why prefer a managed identity over a long-lived application secret for an Azure-hosted workload?
options: It grants every Azure role automatically
It removes the need for application authorization
Azure can issue short-lived tokens without distributing a reusable credential to the workload
It guarantees the data plane is always available
questions.explanation: Managed identity removes routine secret distribution and rotation from the workload. Roles still need least-privilege scope, and the application still enforces business authorization.

questions.question: A deployment succeeds through Azure Resource Manager, but every checkout request returns an error. Which plane should responders investigate first?
options: Only the management-group hierarchy
The workload data plane, including routing, compute, dependencies, identity, and data correctness
Only Azure billing exports
The deployment API because successful deployment proves the application works
questions.explanation: Control-plane success proves the declared management change was accepted. It does not prove that the deployed application can complete its user journey.

questions.question: When is Azure Kubernetes Service a better starting point than a higher-level application platform?
options: Whenever an application uses containers
When the team needs Kubernetes scheduling and ecosystem controls and can own the cluster and workload operating model
Whenever the team wants the fewest operational responsibilities
Only when the application has no networking requirements
questions.explanation: Containers alone do not require Kubernetes. AKS is justified when its control surface solves real requirements and the team can operate upgrades, policy, capacity, security, and workloads.
